concept.name: Macaulay duration
concept.definition: The weighted-average time until a bond's cash flows are received, with each cash flow weighted by its share of the bond's present value. Expressed in years, it equals maturity for a zero-coupon bond and is always shorter than maturity for a coupon bond; it is the foundation from which modified and effective duration are derived.
concept.intuition: It is the 'center of gravity' of a bond's payments — the single point in time at which the average dollar of the bond's value arrives.
concept.mechanics: Each cash flow's present value is divided by the bond's full price to get a weight; the weights are multiplied by the time to receipt and summed. Dividing Macaulay duration by (1 + yield per period) gives modified duration, the direct price-sensitivity measure.
concept.formula: MacDur = Σ_t [ t × PV(CF_t) ] / P, where PV(CF_t) is the present value of the cash flow at time t and P the full price; ModDur = MacDur / (1 + r), with r the yield per period.
concept.failure_modes: As a time measure it applies cleanly only to fixed cash flows; for callable or floating-rate instruments the cash-flow weights are not fixed, so Macaulay duration is undefined or misleading without an options model.
concept.misconceptions: Duration in years is often mistaken for the bond's remaining life; a 10-year coupon bond's Macaulay duration is well below 10 years, and duration (not maturity) is what governs rate sensitivity.
concept.example: A 4-year, 4% semiannual-pay bond at a 6% yield has an annualized Macaulay duration of about 3.72 years — less than its 4-year maturity because coupons arrive earlier.
